questions.stem: Which instrument measures the distance travelled by the sound in experiment 1?

options.text: a trundle wheel
options.explanation: The trundle wheel rolls out distances such as the 100 m gap.

options.text: an oscilloscope
options.explanation: The oscilloscope belongs to the electronic method of experiment 2.

options.text: a wooden block
options.explanation: Blocks make the bang; they measure nothing.

options.text: a stopwatch
options.explanation: A stopwatch measures time, not distance.

questions.stem: Why does the timer start the stopwatch when the blocks are seen to clash, not when they are heard?

options.text: because the bang is too quiet to hear
options.explanation: The bang is the very signal being timed.

options.text: because light travels much faster than sound, so the sight of the bang is effectively instant
options.explanation: Light reaches the timer in a negligible time compared with the sound delay.

options.text: because sound cannot travel more than 100 m
options.explanation: Sound travels any distance; it simply takes time.

options.text: because the stopwatch only responds to light
options.explanation: Stopwatches respond to fingers, not light.

questions.stem: Why is the timing repeated several times and an average taken?

options.text: to calibrate the stopwatch against the trundle wheel
options.explanation: No calibration between instruments happens here.

options.text: to make the bang louder
options.explanation: Averaging cannot change loudness.

options.text: to reduce the effect of random human reaction-time errors
options.explanation: Reaction time varies trial to trial; averaging smooths those random errors.

options.text: to increase the distance the sound travels
options.explanation: Distance is fixed by the measurement, not the repeats.

questions.stem: The experiment is repeated at 120 m, 140 m, 160 m and 180 m. What does plotting distance against average time allow?

options.text: the area under the line gives the speed of sound
options.explanation: Area has no meaning for a distance-time plot here.

options.text: the intercept gives the speed of sound
options.explanation: The intercept is the zero-distance point, not a speed.

options.text: the spread of times to be ignored
options.explanation: Plotting does not remove scatter; it exposes it.

options.text: the gradient of the line gives the speed of sound
options.explanation: Speed is distance over time, which is exactly the gradient of a distance-time graph.

questions.stem: A group measures 180 m between the two points and records an average time of 0.53 s. What speed of sound does this give?

options.text: about 340 m/s
options.explanation: 180 / 0.53 is about 340 m/s, matching the accepted value.

options.text: about 95 m/s
options.explanation: 0.53 / 180 would mix up numerator and denominator.

options.text: about 940 m/s
options.explanation: This is nearly three times too large for air.

options.text: about 53 m/s
options.explanation: This drops the factor of ten and the division.

questions.stem: State the independent and dependent variables of experiment 1.
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the distance between the two points and the dependent variable is the time taken for the sound to travel that distance.

questions.stem: State the equation used in the analysis of the results.
questions.modelAnswer: Average speed = distance moved divided by time taken.

questions.stem: Explain why the stopwatch method gives a less accurate value than the oscilloscope method.
questions.modelAnswer: A human timer must react to seeing and hearing events, and that reaction time is comparable with the travel time of the sound, so the recorded time carries a large random error; the oscilloscope method times the wave electronically, which removes the human reaction delay.

questions.stem: A student suggests timing the bang over a gap of only 2 m with the stopwatch method. Explain whether this is sensible.
questions.modelAnswer: It is not sensible: at about 340 m/s the sound crosses 2 m in roughly 0.006 s, far shorter than any human reaction time, so the stopwatch reading would be almost entirely reaction error; a larger distance makes the travel time comparable with but greater than the reaction uncertainty.

questions.stem: In the oscilloscope method, what triggers the oscilloscope?

options.text: the second microphone detecting the bang
options.explanation: The scope triggers on the FIRST microphone.

options.text: the first microphone detecting the bang
options.explanation: The scope is set to trigger when the first microphone receives the bang.

options.text: the wooden blocks directly
options.explanation: Blocks make sound; they are not connected to the scope.

options.text: the tape measure
options.explanation: The tape measure only fixes the separation.

questions.stem: What does the horizontal separation of the two pulses on the screen represent?

options.text: the frequency of the bang
options.explanation: A single bang is a pulse, not a repeated wave.

options.text: the distance between the microphones
options.explanation: Distance is measured externally with the tape measure.

options.text: the time for the sound to travel from one microphone to the other
options.explanation: The trace offset is the travel time across the gap.

options.text: the amplitude of the bang
options.explanation: Amplitude is the vertical height of the trace.

questions.stem: Which control variable is specific to the oscilloscope method?

options.text: banging the blocks harder each time
options.explanation: That changes conditions rather than controlling them.

options.text: moving the microphones closer each trial
options.explanation: That changes the independent variable.

options.text: using a different oscilloscope each trial
options.explanation: Equipment is kept the same, not varied.

options.text: using the same pair of microphones for every trial
options.explanation: The method declares the same set of microphones as a control variable.

questions.stem: Why is a tape measure used rather than the trundle wheel in the oscilloscope method?

options.text: the separation is small, about 2 m, so a tape measure gives the finer resolution needed
options.explanation: A 2 m gap needs fine measurement; the tape resolution suits it.

options.text: a trundle wheel cannot measure any distance
options.explanation: A trundle wheel measures distance; it is just coarse for 2 m.

options.text: the trundle wheel only works outdoors
options.explanation: Nothing restricts the trundle wheel to outdoors.

options.text: the tape measure times the pulse as well
options.explanation: The tape measures distance only.

questions.stem: Which verdict fairly compares the stopwatch timing with the oscilloscope timing?

options.text: both methods are equally accurate
options.explanation: The electronic method removes the dominant error source.

options.text: the oscilloscope method is better because electronic timing removes human reaction time
options.explanation: Reaction time is the manual method’s weakness and the electronic method removes it.

options.text: the stopwatch method is better because it uses no electricity
options.explanation: Power source is irrelevant to accuracy here.

options.text: neither method can measure the speed of sound
options.explanation: Both are standard measurements with a known result near 340 m/s.

questions.stem: State the independent and dependent variables shared by the two speed-of-sound experiments.
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the distance the sound travels and the dependent variable is the time the sound takes to travel that distance.

questions.stem: State the two quantities the oscilloscope method needs before a speed can be computed.
questions.modelAnswer: The microphone separation (measured with the tape) and the pulse delay read from the screen.

questions.stem: Explain why the microphone separation is kept small in the oscilloscope method.
questions.modelAnswer: A short, precisely measured separation keeps the experiment compact on a bench and lets the oscilloscope display both pulses on one screen with a clear, readable offset, while the electronic timing keeps the error small despite the short travel time.

questions.stem: The microphones are 2.0 m apart and the second pulse arrives 5.9 ms after the first. Calculate the speed of sound and compare it with the accepted value.
questions.modelAnswer: Speed = 2.0 / 0.0059 = about 339 m/s, which is within about 1% of the accepted 340 m/s, so the result supports the accepted value.
